verdict.rationale: Genesis 4:1 makes Adam the grammatical subject of the verb 'knew' (yada, H3045, the marital-intercourse idiom when its subject is a husband and its object his wife) and immediately follows with Eve as subject of 'conceived' (harah, H2029) and 'bore' (yalad, H3205); Cain is named directly in the same clause as the issue of that one act, with no second male agent present. Acts 17:26 makes every nation 'out of one' (ex henos, G1537 plus genitive G1520) and Romans 5:12 routes sin into the world 'through one man' (di henos anthropou, G1223 plus G0444), a one-source grammar. The apostolic interpretive gloss on the seed motif is fixed by 1 John 3:10-12, where the same 'from' (ek) paternity formula is used for both 'children of God' (tekna tou theou, G5043 + G2316) and 'children of the devil' (tekna tou diabolou, G5043 + G1228), all sides reading both as spiritual, and Cain (Kain, G2535) is called 'the brother' (adelphon, G0080) of Abel whom he slew, presupposing shared parentage. John 8:44 applies the same 'you are from the father, the devil' (hymeis ek tou patros tou diabolou, G1537 + G3962 + G1228) to people whom verse 37 has already conceded are Abraham's biological 'seed' (sperma), proving the construction is moral, not biological. 1 Timothy 2:14 labels Eve's transgression 'deception' (apate, G0538) and 'transgression' (parabasis, G3847), not sexual congress.

scripture.reasoning: Adam ('the man', ha-adam) is the subject of the verb 'knew' (yada) with his wife (ishto) as object, then Eve is subject of 'conceived' (harah) and 'bore' (yalad), and Cain (Qayin, H7014B) is the named issue. With a husband as subject and his wife as object, 'knew' (yada) functions as the fixed Hebrew idiom for marital intercourse, and the wayyiqtol chain (the Hebrew narrative 'and then, and then' verb sequence) in the clause string locks the begetting between the two named human parents with no other male agent introduced. Eve's exclamation 'I have gotten a man with the LORD' (qaniti ish eth YHWH) uses the verb 'gotten, acquired' (qanah) with the particle 'eth' read as 'with the help of', crediting the LORD's (YHWH's) enabling, not paternity. The serpent does not appear in the verse.

Adam 'knew' (yada) his wife again, she 'bore' (yalad) Seth, and the verse names Cain (H7014B) explicitly as the brother whom Seth replaces because Cain had slain Abel. The same word chain (yada then yalad) that produced Cain in Genesis 4:1 produces Seth here, treating Cain, Abel, and Seth as one sibling set from one couple. Cain as Seth's brother in the syntax presupposes shared parentage with Adam and Eve.

Adam 'begot' (yalad) in his own 'likeness' (demuth) and after his 'image' (tselem), the two words that Genesis 1:26 used for the human creation in God's image. The genealogy of Genesis 5 traces all subsequent humanity through Adam by this same begetting verb 'begot' (yalad), with no parallel line introduced. Every named human descends from one Adamic stock.

Adam names his wife 'Eve' (Chavvah, H2332, a word occurring only once in this verse and once in Genesis 4:1 in the entire Bible) because she was 'mother of all living' (em kol chai). The clause makes Eve the universal matriarch of every living human, ruling out parallel non-Adamic human lineages by definition.

'He made out of one every nation of men' (epoiesen te ex henos pan ethnos anthropon). The prepositional phrase 'out of one' (ex henos, the noun in the 'from-X' grammatical form for 'one' (heis) governed by the preposition 'from' (ek)) marks one human source for the whole of humanity, and 'every nation of men' (pan ethnos anthropon) makes the scope total. This forecloses divergent racial lineages with separate or satanic origins.

'Through one man sin entered into the world' (di henos anthropou he hamartia eis ton kosmon eiselthen). The instrumental 'through' (dia) plus 'of one man' (henos anthropou in the 'from-X' grammatical form) names one human being as the single conduit of sin and death for all, and verse 14 explicitly names that one man Adam (G0076). The argument presupposes one head over the whole race, not multiple seed-lines.

'Through the disobedience of the one man the many were constituted sinners' (dia tes parakoes tou henos anthropou hamartoloi katestathesan hoi polloi). Eden's transgression is named 'disobedience' (parakoe), not any sexual act, and the single head produces the entire constituency of sinners.

'The woman, being deceived, came to be in transgression' (he gyne exapatetheisa en parabasei gegonen). Eve's Eden act is labeled lexically as 'deception' (apate) and 'transgression' (parabasis, a transgression of a command), the standard moral-cognitive vocabulary, not a sexual term. Where a sexual encounter was intended, biblical Greek has explicit verbs ('to know' in a marital sense (ginosko), 'to be with' (suneimi), 'to lie with' (koitazomai)); none appears here or in Genesis 3.

'In the Adam all die' (en to Adam pantes apothneskousin). The universal 'all' (pantes) is grounded in the one Adam, parallel to 'in the Christ all will be made alive' (en to Christo pantes zoopoiethesontai). Adam as the single federal head (the one-man covenant representative for the whole race) of all dying humanity rules out parallel non-Adamic human lines.

'Of Adam, of God' (tou Adam tou theou). The genealogy of Jesus terminates at Adam, and Adam at God, making one continuous descent from God through one originating man to the Christ. No parallel non-Adamic line is registered in the canon's only complete back-to-origin genealogy.

complicating_texts.resolution: The 'seed' (zera, H2233) language sets enmity between the serpent's 'seed' (zera) and the woman's 'seed' (zera). The word 'seed' (zera) carries two attested senses across the canon: literal biological offspring (Genesis 15:5, Genesis 17:7) and figurative posterity or line of allegiance (Isaiah 1:4 'seed of evildoers' (zera mereim), a brood of evildoers; Isaiah 57:4 'seed of falsehood' (zera sheker)). The syntax of Genesis 3:15 supplies no verb of sexual relations between the serpent and the woman; the verse names 'enmity' (eyvah, H0342) and a head-heel strike ('bruise' (shuph) H7779 plus 'heel' (aqeb) H6119), not begetting. Read against 1 John 3:8-12, where the same hostility is named as belonging to those 'from the devil' (ek tou diabolou) and those 'from God' (ek tou theou), the canon ranks 'seed' (zera) here as figurative line of allegiance, not literal physical paternity by the serpent.

The clause 'I have gotten a man with the LORD' (qaniti ish eth YHWH) has been read by serpent-seed proponents as Eve crediting a being other than Adam for Cain. The preceding clause already supplies Adam as the father by the verb 'knew' (yada) plus 'his wife' (ishto), the standard marital-intercourse idiom, so Eve's exclamation cannot grammatically displace the father just established. The particle 'eth' in 'I have gotten a man with the LORD' (qaniti ish eth YHWH) is best read as the preposition 'with' (et, 'with the help of'), a common Hebrew use, which credits the LORD's (YHWH's) enabling, not paternity. Read with Genesis 4:25, where Adam again 'knows' (yada) his wife and 'bears' (yalad) Seth and Cain is explicitly named as the brother who slew Abel, Cain stands as Adam's biological son.

Cain is said to be 'from the evil one' (ek tou ponerou). The multiple meanings of 'from' (ek) paternity language are resolved within the same paragraph: verse 10 contrasts 'the children of God' (ta tekna tou theou) and 'the children of the devil' (ta tekna tou diabolou), and no reader holds that the children of God are biologically begotten by God in the flesh, so the 'from' (ek) paternity formula must be moral and relational on both sides. The same verse then calls Cain 'the brother' (adelphos) of Abel whom he slew, presupposing shared biological parentage with Abel and Adam. The paragraph itself ranks 'from' (ek) as moral, not biological.

'You are from the father, the devil' (hymeis ek tou patros tou diabolou este). Spoken to people whom Jesus has explicitly granted in verse 37 are Abraham's 'seed' (sperma), the construction 'from' (ek) plus 'father' (pater) plus the 'from-X' grammatical form cannot be biological without contradicting verse 37. The very same chapter therefore ranks 'from the father, the devil' (ek tou patros tou diabolou) as a moral and volitional paternity ('the desires of your father you will to do', verse 44), the same lens 1 John 3:10-12 supplies. This forecloses any literal-paternity reading of seed-of-the-serpent language.

variants.note: Anchor verses span Genesis 3 to 5 (Old Testament, no critical edition of New Testament textual variants in scope), Acts 17:26, Romans 5:12-19, 1 Corinthians 15:22, Luke 3:38, 1 Timothy 2:14, John 8:44, and 1 John 3:8-12 (New Testament outside the 3 John sample of the modern coherence-based genealogical method). No variant unit in the standard apparatus alters the 'knew then conceived then bore' (yada-harah-yalad) chain in Genesis 4:1, the 'out of one' (ex henos) in Acts 17:26, or the 'through one man' (di henos anthropou) in Romans 5:12. The verdict does not turn on any disputed reading.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Genesis 4:1 'knew' (yada) plus 'wife' (ishah) is the marital-intercourse idiom with Adam as subject; Acts 17:26 'out of one' (ex henos) and Romans 5:12 'through one man' (di henos anthropou) name a single human origin and head. 1 Timothy 2:14 labels Eve's act 'deception' (apate) and 'transgression' (parabasis), not sexual congress. The serpent never governs a begetting verb.

The Adam-Christ federal (covenant-representative) parallel in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 requires one human head over the whole race. A bifurcated bloodline (split into two parallel lines) with a satanic branch would disable both the universal scope of the fall and the universal scope of the second-Adam remedy.

The typological reading of 'seed' (zera) in Genesis 3:15 as the woman's line culminating in the Messiah, opposed by the serpent's line as those who morally side with him, is the reading 1 John 3:8-12 explicitly canonicalizes (the one doing sin is 'from the devil' (ek tou diabolou); Cain is 'from the evil one' (ek tou ponerou)). Typology (a pattern in earlier Scripture that prefigures a later reality) here is spiritual paternity, not biological.

The serpent-seed lens reads 'seed' (zera) in Genesis 3:15 as literal biological offspring and 'I have gotten a man with the LORD' (qaniti ish eth YHWH) in Genesis 4:1 as Eve crediting another being for Cain. On its own terms it claims the word forms (morphology) of Genesis 4:1 leave room for a non-Adamic father. The lens fails on the lexical data because verse 1a already supplies Adam as the father via 'knew' (yada) plus 'his wife' (ishto), because Genesis 4:25 repeats the same chain to produce Seth while naming Cain as brother, and because 1 John 3:10 uses the identical 'from' (ek) paternity formula for 'children of God' (tekna tou theou, which all sides agree is non-biological), ranking the construction moral on both sides of the parallel.

hermeneutics.notes: Verdict rests on plain word forms (morphology) and sentence structure (syntax). The multiple meanings of 'seed' (zera, literal seed vs figurative posterity) and of 'from' (ek) paternity (origin vs moral allegiance) are resolved within the canon itself by 1 John 3:10's parallel use of 'children of God' (tekna tou theou) and John 8:44's address to those already conceded to be Abraham's 'seed' (sperma).

stem_audit.notes: The stem denies a specific heterodox claim (serpent-seed or dual-seed anthropology, sometimes carrying racist applications). It states three lexically checkable propositions: Eden's transgression was disobedience, Cain is the natural son of Adam, and all humanity descends from one originating pair. These are testable against the word forms (morphology) of Genesis 4:1, Genesis 4:25, Genesis 5:3, Genesis 3:20, Acts 17:26, Romans 5:12-19, 1 Corinthians 15:22, Luke 3:38, 1 Timothy 2:14, John 8:44, and 1 John 3:8-12, so no neutralization was required.

lay_summary: The question denies the serpent-seed or dual-seed claim that Eve had sexual relations with the serpent or with Satan, that Cain was the offspring of that union, and that humanity then split into separate bloodlines, one of them traceable to Satan. The Hebrew of Genesis 4:1 settles the paternity directly. Adam 'knew' (yada) Eve his wife, she 'conceived' (harah) and 'bore' (yalad) Cain. With a husband as subject of 'knew' (yada) and his wife as object, this is the fixed Hebrew way of describing marital relations, and the verb chain locks the begetting between the two named human parents with no other male agent introduced. Eve's words, often rendered 'I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD', use the verb 'to get or acquire' (qanah) and credit God's enabling, not the serpent's fathering. The same verb chain reappears in Genesis 4:25 to produce Seth, and the verse names Cain explicitly as the brother whom Seth replaces, presupposing shared parents. Genesis 5:3 then traces all later humanity through Adam by the same begetting verb in Adam's own likeness and image. Where confusion arises is around two words. The Hebrew word 'seed' (zera) can mean either literal offspring or a figurative line of allegiance (as in 'seed of evildoers', Isaiah 1:4), and the Greek phrase 'from the father' (ek tou patros) can describe biological origin or moral allegiance. The canon itself ranks the meaning. In 1 John 3:10-12 the same 'from' (ek) formula labels both 'children of God' and 'children of the devil', and no reader holds that the children of God are physically begotten by God in the flesh, so the construction is moral and relational on both sides. The same passage then calls Cain the brother of Abel he killed, presupposing they shared parents. In John 8:44 Jesus tells opponents they are 'of their father the devil', even though He has just granted (verse 37) that they are Abraham's biological 'seed', so again the construction is spiritual, not biological. In the New Testament, Acts 17:26 says God made 'out of one' (ex henos) every nation of men, and Romans 5:12 and 19 say sin and death entered 'through one man' (di henos anthropou) by his 'disobedience' (parakoe), with 1 Timothy 2:14 naming Eve's act 'deception' (apate) and 'transgression' (parabasis), not sexual congress. Across both testaments the lexical pattern supports one originating human pair and an Eden transgression of disobedience, and gives no grammatical foothold for a satanic bloodline.
